title: Typewriter and Clock
premise: In the winter of 1939, as the Republic of Verlaine collapses under advancing armies, Edmund Amberdale carries diplomatic pouches and coded dispatches for a government already negotiating its own surrender. When an infant is abandoned at his safehouse boardinghouse with a note ordering him to forget the child's face, Edmund cannot—her eyes belong to a woman he loved and lost in the purge of the Foreign Ministry. Smuggling the girl past three military checkpoints alongside the documents that could expose the republic's betrayers, Edmund is forced to choose between duty, survival, and belonging. The book ends with Edmund burning his own identity papers, delivering the evidence not to the dying government but to a neutral journalist, and crossing the border as a nameless man with a daughter who will one day carry his true name.
about_author: Mara Dunmore is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing diplomatic correspondence from interwar Europe, where she first encountered the marginalia of couriers who never made it home. She writes from a converted mill in Vermont, where she keeps her grandmother's typewriter and an unsynchronized collection of clocks.

chapters.title: The Weight of Orders
chapters.summary: Edmund Amberdale, courier for a collapsing republic, receives his final assignment: carry sealed dispatches from the capital to the border legation. His POV establishes his philosophy—carry only what can be carried, feel nothing, be no one. Emotional beat: disciplined detachment masking exhaustion as the city empties around him.

chapters.title: A Boardinghouse of Strangers
chapters.summary: Edmund takes a room at Madame Kessler's boardinghouse, the last safehouse on his route. Through his eyes we meet the other lodgers: a defrocked priest, a wounded soldier, a pianist who plays only after curfew. Emotional beat: the strange comfort of temporary company among people trained not to ask questions.

chapters.title: What the Ministry Burned
chapters.summary: At the Foreign Ministry, Edmund collects his pouches and witnesses clerks feeding ledgers into a furnace—erasing names, debts, betrayals. He glimpses a page he shouldn't: signatures of men now leading the invading delegation. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: the first crack in his obedience; some things burned refuse to stay ash.

chapters.title: The Knock at Midnight
chapters.summary: A woman's voice in the alley, a bundle pressed into his arms, and a note in handwriting he recognizes: 'Forget the face.' Inside the blanket, an infant. Edmund recognizes the eyes of Lise Marchand, the translator he loved before the purges took her. Emotional beat: his carefully built invisibility shatters in a single held breath.

chapters.title: Instructions for Forgetting
chapters.summary: Edmund deciphers the note's cipher: the child is Lise's, the evidence of the betrayal is sewn into the blanket's hem, and Lise is dead or worse. His POV wars between the courier's creed and the father he never admitted to being. Emotional beat: grief arriving years late, in the shape of a hungry infant.

chapters.title: Madame Kessler's Silence
chapters.summary: Madame Kessler discovers the child but asks nothing; instead she leaves milk and an old cradle. Through her brief POV we learn she lost a son to the last war and recognizes what Edmund cannot say. Emotional beat: unspoken alliance—belonging offered without conditions, which terrifies Edmund more than the checkpoints.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Edmund maps his route: the river bridge, the rail yard, the mountain pass—each held by different forces with different loyalties. He rehearses his cover as a commercial clerk. Emotional beat: dread converted into procedure, the courier's discipline stretched over a heart now beating for two.

chapters.title: The Pianist's Bargain
chapters.summary: The lodger-pianist, Anselm, reveals he is a deserter who knows the rail yard guards and offers passage in exchange for Edmund carrying his own sealed confession to a sister abroad. POV shifts to Anselm. Emotional beat: two men trading secrets, discovering trust is also cargo that can be carried.

chapters.title: Lise's Letters
chapters.summary: Hidden in the blanket's lining, Edmund finds Lise's unsent letters—her recruitment as a translator, what she learned, why she ran. Through her letters, her voice enters the novel. Emotional beat: falling in love again with a dead woman, and understanding she trusted him with everything at the end.

chapters.title: Curfew, With a Child
chapters.summary: A routine curfew sweep forces Edmund to hide the infant during an inspection of the boardinghouse. Madame Kessler performs a small theatrical deception with the priest's collar and a christening story. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into absurd tenderness; the household becomes, for one night, a family of liars.

chapters.title: The River Bridge
chapters.summary: First checkpoint: Edmund crosses the river bridge with documents in his boot and the baby drugged with Kessler's laudanum, a decision that shames him. The guard is a boy who checks nothing. POV: Edmund. Emotional beat: relief curdling into guilt—he has sedated his daughter to save her.

chapters.title: What the Dispatches Say
chapters.summary: Edmund finally decodes the dispatches he carries: the republic's inner council has arranged capitulation in exchange for immunity, selling the army and the ministries. He is not a courier; he is an accessory. Emotional beat: the vertigo of realizing his duty was always someone else's crime.

chapters.title: Anselm's Confession
chapters.summary: Anselm, feverish from his wound, tells Edmund what his sealed letter contains: he fired on civilians under orders and cannot live unconfessed. POV: Anselm's final night. Emotional beat: Edmund recognizes his own evasion in Anselm's honesty, and it stings like a rebuke.

chapters.title: The Rail Yard at Dawn
chapters.summary: Second checkpoint: Anselm's contact waves them through a freight yard, but a counterintelligence officer arrives unannounced and holds Edmund's papers too long. The baby wakes. Emotional beat: a held breath, a cry muffled against Edmund's chest, and the officer's eyes that see too much and let it go—for a price to be named later.

chapters.title: The Price
chapters.summary: The officer, Captain Voss, finds Edmund at the next town and makes his offer: the documents in exchange for passage and silence. He suspects what Edmund carries but not where. Emotional beat: corruption wearing a courteous face; Edmund learns the enemy is not an army but an appetite.

chapters.title: A Name for the Child
chapters.summary: In a church crypt, sheltering from a bombardment, Edmund names the baby Lise, after her mother, breaking his own rule against leaving traces. POV: Edmund, speaking to the sleeping child. Emotional beat: the moment he stops being a courier and becomes a father—naming is the first act of belonging.

chapters.title: The Priest's Road
chapters.summary: The defrocked priest, Father Ivo, guides them along smugglers' paths he once used for fugitives. Through his POV we learn the boardinghouse network was always a resistance of small mercies. Emotional beat: Edmund discovers he was never as alone or as neutral as he believed—everyone was carrying something.

chapters.title: Bombardment
chapters.summary: The advancing army shells the town where they shelter; Father Ivo is killed pulling children from a collapsing tenement. Emotional beat: the cost of staying visible; Edmund buries the priest with his collar and understands that neutrality is a luxury already repossessed.

chapters.title: Voss Closes In
chapters.summary: Captain Voss intercepts the refugee column, searching for a courier with a child. Edmund hides the dispatches in Anselm's coffin as the column buries its dead. Emotional beat: grief weaponized—Voss's suspicion defeated by genuine mourning he cannot distinguish from deception.

chapters.title: The Legation Burns
chapters.summary: Reaching the border legation, Edmund finds it evacuated and burning; his official orders are now worthless paper. The destination his whole identity was built toward has ceased to exist. Emotional beat: the strange freedom of a mission with no destination—duty dissolved, choice remains.

chapters.title: What Duty Means Now
chapters.summary: Edmund takes stock: the evidence, the child, Anselm's confession, and a choice between delivering the documents to the traitors' new regime or to a neutral journalist at the border town of Halst. Emotional beat: the courier's creed rewritten—some things must be carried to the truth, not to the address.

chapters.title: The Journalist
chapters.summary: Edmund makes contact with Ruth Aldervik, a neutral correspondent who has been documenting the capitulation. She tests him, suspects a trap, and demands the full story. POV alternates between Ruth's skepticism and Edmund's confession. Emotional beat: being believed for the first time—the relief and terror of testimony.

chapters.title: Anselm's Letter, Delivered
chapters.summary: Edmund finds Anselm's sister in Halst and delivers the sealed confession. She reads it, weeps, and tells Edmund her brother was the gentlest of four. Emotional beat: a debt discharged; Edmund learns that carrying someone's truth can be a form of love.

chapters.title: Voss at the Border
chapters.summary: Voss reaches Halst with authority to detain anyone crossing. He corners Edmund at the checkpoint inn and names his price again: the documents for two exit visas. Emotional beat: temptation with a human face—Voss is not a monster, which makes refusing harder.

chapters.title: The Third Checkpoint
chapters.summary: The mountain pass: Edmund attempts the crossing with Lise hidden in a smuggler's cart while Ruth's press credentials cover his papers. Voss waits at the barrier. Emotional beat: the climax begins—every skill of invisibility deployed at once, for the opposite of invisibility: to be seen and believed.

chapters.title: The Search
chapters.summary: Voss orders the cart searched. The smuggler's diversion, Ruth's intervention as press, and the crying child herself—whom Voss, unexpectedly, will not order harmed—buy Edmund seconds. POV: Voss, for one chapter, a man serving an appetite he no longer believes in. Emotional beat: the enemy's crack of doubt.

chapters.title: Over the Pass
chapters.summary: Edmund and Lise cross on foot through the storm with the dispatches sewn into Edmund's own coat, beside his skin. He burns his identity papers at the ridge line. Emotional beat: burning the self he was; the courier dies on the mountain, the father crosses.

chapters.title: Halst, Neutral Ground
chapters.summary: In Halst, Ruth publishes the evidence; the capitulation deal collapses into scandal, and the traitors' immunity evaporates. Edmund watches the newsstand crowds from a window, anonymous at last by choice. Emotional beat: the mission completed on his own terms—duty fulfilled against the orders that defined it.

chapters.title: Voss's Last Visit
chapters.summary: Voss, disgraced but unprosecuted, finds Edmund and asks not for the documents but for the truth: was it worth it? Edmund answers with the sleeping child on his shoulder. Emotional beat: an enemy's quiet surrender; some defeats are a kind of release.

chapters.title: The Face Remembered
chapters.summary: Edmund writes Lise Marchand's full story for Ruth's archive—her name, her courage, her daughter—refusing the instruction to forget the face. Emotional beat: memory as an act of defiance; the opposite of the order he received.

chapters.title: A Room of Her Own
chapters.summary: Edmund and Lise settle in Halst's exile quarter; he takes work as a translator's clerk, the trade Lise loved. The boardinghouse lodgers' fates arrive in letters—Anselm's sister visits, Kessler survives. Emotional beat: the scattered family reassembling into a new, chosen shape.

chapters.title: The Clock Without a Pendulum
chapters.summary: Edmund buys a broken clock from the market and repairs it, keeping it deliberately unsynchronized with every other clock in the house. POV: Edmund, reflective. Emotional beat: time measured no longer by orders and deadlines but by a child's growing—his own time, finally.

chapters.title: The Typewriter
chapters.summary: Ruth gives Edmund her old typewriter and suggests he write what he knows: the couriers, the boardinghouses, the small mercies. He begins the manuscript that becomes this book. Emotional beat: turning witness into word; the last cargo is a story, and it is deliverable.

chapters.title: A Letter from the Capital
chapters.summary: A letter arrives from a surviving Foreign Ministry clerk: Lise's final hours, and confirmation that she named Edmund on her last document. Emotional beat: grief and gift in one envelope—she chose him, knowing the cost; his belonging was never in doubt from her side.

chapters.title: Lise Learns Her Name
chapters.summary: The child, now walking and talking, asks about her name. Edmund tells her the truth in the words a toddler can hold: her mother was brave, and brave people leave marks. Emotional beat: the first handing-down of memory; inheritance begins with a bedtime story.

chapters.title: The Old Creed
chapters.summary: A former colleague from the courier service finds Edmund, still carrying orders for a government that no longer exists, and asks him to come back. Edmund declines. Emotional beat: the past offering him his old self back, and the quiet strength of refusing it.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Edmund sorts his belongings into one case—the courier's discipline transformed: carry only what matters, and what matters is a child, a manuscript, a name. Emotional beat: the book's philosophy made flesh; the inventory of a life pared to its truth.

chapters.title: The Border, Years Later
chapters.summary: Edmund takes Lise to the pass where they crossed, now a peaceful checkpoint between friendly towns. He shows her the ridge where papers burned. POV: Edmund, with Lise's small voice asking questions. Emotional beat: return without fear; the geography of survival becomes the geography of memory.

chapters.title: The Last Page
chapters.summary: Edmund finishes the manuscript and types the dedication: 'For Lise, who was told to forget the face, and never did.' He mails it to Ruth. Emotional beat: completion and release—the courier's final delivery is the truth itself, signed at last with his real name.

chapters.title: Typewriter and Clock
chapters.summary: Years on: the published book arrives at the Halst house; adult Lise reads her own origin in its pages while Edmund keeps time by his one unsynchronized clock. Emotional beat: resolution—memory kept, belonging chosen, love that outlasted duty, and a story that carried them all across every border.
